bakong.km: ប្រាសាទបាគង
bakong.by: Photographs by Samnang Loy · Roluos, Siem Reap, Cambodia
d: Bakong stands in the Roluos group near Siem Reap, where the early Khmer capital Hariharalaya once stood. King Indravarman I made it his state temple and dedicated it to Shiva in 881 CE, long before Angkor Wat was built.

It is one of the first great temple-mountains of the Khmer Empire. A sandstone pyramid rises in five levels to the sanctuary at the top. Stone lions guard the stairways, and stone elephants stand at the corners of the lower terraces.

Two moats surround the temple. You cross them on a long causeway lined with seven-headed naga balustrades, among the earliest of their kind in Khmer architecture. From the water, the tower appears between the palm trees.

The tower on the summit is not from the ninth century. It was added later, in the 12th century. In the 1930s, the French conservator Maurice Glaize restored the pyramid by taking it apart and rebuilding it stone by stone.

Look closely at the summit tower: graceful devatas (female guardian figures) stand in niches, wearing pleated skirts and jewellery. Some carved blocks no longer line up, so a figure’s head and body may sit on different stones.
bakong.l: The five levels of the pyramid · the stone lions on the stairways · the carved lintel of the eastern gateway framing the tower · the devatas around the summit tower · the moat with its palm trees.

banteaysrei.km: ប្រាសាទបន្ទាយស្រី
banteaysrei.by: Photographs by Samnang Loy · Siem Reap, Cambodia
f: Yajnavaraha, a Brahmin advisor, and his brother Vishnukumara
d: Banteay Srei is a small temple north of the main Angkor temples, famous for the finest stone carving in Khmer art. Its name is often translated as “citadel of women” or “citadel of beauty.”

According to its foundation inscription, it was founded in 967 CE during the reign of King Rajendravarman II. Unlike most great temples, it was not built by a king but by his Brahmin advisor Yajnavaraha and his brother Vishnukumara, and was dedicated to Shiva.
The temple is built of pink sandstone, which turns warm orange and red in the afternoon sun. Three small towers stand in the centre, and the walls and gateways are covered in deep, lace-like carving.
Look up at the triangular pediments: rows of flame-like leaves, lotus flowers in diamond frames, and at the ends, great curling tails shaped like waves.

The temple was rediscovered in 1914. In 1923 the French writer André Malraux was caught trying to take carved devatas away. From 1931, Henri Marchal restored it by anastylosis, putting the original stones back in place.

Inside, the carvings tell stories. One pediment shows a scene from the Ramayana: the monkey brothers Vali and Sugriva fighting, while Rama aims his bow. Another, from the Mahabharata, shows the god Indra on his three-headed elephant sending rain over the burning Khandava forest, full of fleeing animals. On another pediment, Narasimha, the lion-man form of Vishnu, tears apart the demon king Hiranyakashipu.

Kneeling guardian figures with animal heads sit beside the stairs of the central shrines, and graceful devatas smile from their niches. Even the false doors are carved stone, covered with tiny flowers and patterns.
banteaysrei.l: The three central towers · the curling pediment ends against the sky · the lotus flowers in diamond frames · the deep pink colour of the stone · the tall white tree behind the temple.
